screens.title: Understanding Attributes and Groups
screens.narratorSegment: In Houdini, geometry is just half the story. The other half is the data attached to that geometry — attributes. In this lesson you will learn what attributes are, the four classes they belong to, and how groups let you target portions of a mesh non-destructively. Attributes are values stored on points, primitives, vertices, or on the entire geometry. They control color, texture coordinates, normals, velocities and even custom integers or strings that downstream nodes or renderers can read. You will also add a detail attribute to record project metadata, demonstrating how attributes and groups combine to make procedural modeling precise and maintainable. By the end, you’ll understand when to use point versus vertex attributes, how to avoid the common mistake of choosing the wrong attribute class, and how groups help keep your networks readable and flexible.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Understanding Attributes and Groups
Understanding Attributes and Groups
How geometry carries data and how to target parts of a mesh

Attributes are pieces of data attached to geometry. Groups name selections so you can apply operations to only those components. Both are essential to procedural modeling and simulations because they let you control behavior without manual edits.

In this lesson
Identify attribute classes and create attributes with Attribute Create SOP.
Coming up

Why it matters
Attributes + groups make your node networks flexible and data-driven.
Visual concept
Attributes (P, N, Cd, uv) + Groups (named masks)
Point / Primitive / Vertex / Detail — each stores data at a different geometric granularity.
Groups let nodes operate only on selected components, like extruding only the panels in a named group.

screens.title: What are attributes?
screens.narratorSegment: Attributes are structured pieces of data stored on geometry components — they are not visual by themselves, but they inform how geometry looks and behaves. In Houdini, attributes can be vectors like position or color, integers, floats, or strings. The important claim is this: attributes make geometry data-driven. For example, the position attribute named P stores X, Y, Z coordinates and is updated whenever you move a point. A normal attribute N stores a surface direction used for shading and certain deformations. Color, Cd, is typically a three-component vector used by renderers or the viewport color display. Attribute types matter because they determine how downstream nodes interpret values; a vector cannot be treated the same as an integer. A concrete example: if you set Cd as a vertex attribute with different RGB values per face, the Color SOP can visualize that and a renderer will pick up those colors per vertex interpolation. A common misconception is thinking attributes are permanent or locked; they are simply data that nodes can read and overwrite. Another misconception is that attributes are only for rendering — they also control simulation parameters, instancing IDs, and export metadata. Key takeaway: think of attributes as the flexible data layer that lives on top of geometry and unlocks procedural control. How would you use a custom attribute to control the height of an extrusion? Consider where that value should be stored — point, primitive, vertex, or detail — before you create it.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Attributes are named data attached to geometry that nodes read and write to control appearance and behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What are attributes?
Attributes: the data layer
Named values stored on geometry components
Attributes define geometry behavior. They are typed and scoped. Common attribute roles include:
  • P — position vector with X, Y, Z coordinates.
  • N — normal vector used for shading and direction-based operations.
  • Cd — color vector for RGB values.
  • uv — 2D texture coordinate stored as a vector of size 2.
Analogy
Attributes are like tags or spreadsheet columns attached to geometry rows; you can filter, sort, and act on them downstream.
Concrete example
Assign Cd as a vertex attribute for a face so each face can have a different color even when points are shared.
// Visual: Attribute Create settings
Class: Vertex
Name: Cd
Type: Vector
Size: 3
Value: 1, 0, 0  // red for that group's vertices
Key Takeaway

Attributes are flexible; match class and type to the role you need so downstream nodes behave correctly.

screens.title: The four attribute classes
screens.narratorSegment: Houdini organizes attributes into four classes tied to geometric components. Point attributes live on points. They are ideal for storing properties that should remain consistent for a point across all primitives that reference it, such as position, or a point-level weight. Primitive attributes are stored per primitive, like a material ID for a face or a primitive-wide flag. Use primitive attributes when the value represents an entire polygon or curve segment. Vertex attributes are stored per vertex, the combination of a point and a primitive; because of this they are essential when a shared point must carry different values per face, for instance unique UVs or vertex colors. A final class, detail attributes, is stored once for the whole geometry and is appropriate for global parameters such as a project_version or a single timestamp. A concrete scenario: to give each face of a cube a different UV layout, use vertex attributes; to mark an entire face as 'damaged' use a primitive attribute. A common misconception is that point attributes always give more precision — they do not; vertex attributes give independent data per face at shared points. When deciding where to store a value, ask: should this data vary per-primitive, per-point, per-vertex, or be global? That question usually reveals the correct class.

keyIdea.title: Class decision rule
keyIdea.text: Ask whether the data must vary per point, per primitive, per vertex (point+primitive), or be global. Use that answer to pick the class.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › The four attribute classes
Class comparison
Choose the class that matches your desired data granularity
Point
Stored per point. Use for position and point-wide properties.
Primitive
Stored per primitive. Use for material IDs or face-level flags.
Vertex
Stored per vertex (point+primitive). Use for UVs or per-face vertex colors on shared points.
Detail
Single value for the whole geometry. Use for project_version or global scale factors.
Quick decision flow
  1. Does it vary per face even when points are shared? Use Vertex.
  2. Is it a property of a whole polygon? Use Primitive.
  3. Is it tied to a point location or velocity? Use Point.
  4. Is it a single global value? Use Detail.
Misconception check: vertex is not the same as point — vertex stores the combination of point and primitive.

screens.title: Common built-in attributes: P, N, Cd, uv, v
screens.narratorSegment: Several built-in attributes appear in most Houdini workflows. Position, named P, is a three-component vector representing a point's coordinates in space; moving a point changes P. Normal, N, is also a vector that indicates surface orientation and is heavily used by shading and orientation-sensitive operations. Cd is the conventional color attribute; it is typically a vector of three components (RGB) and can be stored as point, primitive or vertex depending on the needed variation. The uv attribute stores 2D texture coordinates and is commonly a vector of size two; because textures often differ per-face at shared points, uv is frequently stored as a vertex attribute. Velocity, often denoted v, is a vector used in simulation contexts to represent motion and is usually a point attribute when per-point motion is needed. Understanding the semantics and expected type for each built-in attribute helps you avoid mismatches — for instance, a shader will expect Cd to be present and named correctly, while UV mapping tools expect uv in the right class. A practical example: if you set a vertex Cd per face, the viewport displays each face in its color after you apply Color from Attributes. Misconception to watch: Cd stored as a detail attribute will not give per-face color; detail is global and unsuitable for per-component variations.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Built-in attributes
Common attribute roles
How built-ins are typically used
P — position
Vector3. Stores point coordinates.
N — normal
Vector3. Surface orientation for shading and directional ops.
Cd — color
Vector3. RGB values, often Vertex for per-face colors.
uv — texture coord
Vector2. UV layout, often stored per vertex to vary across faces.
v — velocity
Vector3. Used by simulations; typically per-point when representing motion per vertex position.
Quick example
Set Cd as Vertex for red on a face: Attribute Create → Class: Vertex → Name: Cd → Type: Vector → Value: 1,0,0
Misconception check: detail Cd will not color per-face; it is a single color for the whole geometry.

screens.title: Using the Attribute Create SOP
screens.narratorSegment: The Attribute Create SOP is the tool you use when you want to make a new attribute or set default values for an existing one. Its key parameters you must set deliberately are Class, Name, Type, Size, Value, and optionally Group. Class selects the attribute scope — point, primitive, vertex, or detail. Name is the attribute identifier, like Cd or project_version. Type and Size define whether the attribute is integer, float, string or vector and how many components it holds. Value sets the default or constant written by the node. The Group parameter scopes the write to only those components belonging to a named selection. A typical workflow is: create a Group SOP to build the selection; place Attribute Create after it and type the group name into Attribute Create's Group field so only that selection receives the new attribute. For example, to color a face red: set Class to Vertex, Name to Cd, Type to Vector, Size to 3, Value to 1,0,0, and set Group to face_red. A common mistake is forgetting to set Class correctly — if you choose Point instead of Vertex, shared points will force the same color across faces. Another subtlety: when creating detail attributes, Size still matters; a single integer detail uses Size 1. Always inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet after creating attributes to confirm class, type and values. That quick check saves time debugging downstream nodes that expect attributes in a particular scope.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Attribute Create SOP
Attribute Create parameters
What each field controls
Class — pick point, primitive, vertex, or detail.
Name — attribute identifier, e.g., Cd or project_version.
Type & Size — integer, float, string, or vector components.
Value — the default value to write for the attribute.

Practical example
// To color a face red for only that face's vertices
Class: Vertex
Name: Cd
Type: Vector
Size: 3

screens.title: Hands-on: color faces on a box
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the box example step by step so you can run it yourself and immediately see attributes appear. Start with a Box SOP and dive inside the geometry context. Add a Group SOP and set Group Type to Primitives. In the viewport select a single face and name the group face_red. This creates a named selection that other nodes can reference. Next add an Attribute Create SOP. Choose Class = Vertex, Name = Cd, Type = Vector, Size = 3, and set Value = 1,0,0. In Attribute Create's Group field, type face_red so the write only affects vertices belonging to that face. Repeat the Group + Attribute Create steps to create face_blue with Cd = 0,0,1. Then add a Color SOP set to From Attributes to visualize. Finally open the Geometry Spreadsheet to inspect vertex rows and confirm Cd values on the vertices that belong to your face groups. A common confusion is expecting point-level Cd to let two faces sharing a point have different colors — that will not work. The vertex class is required for per-face color when points are shared. The practical takeaway is to build your selection with groups, then write attributes scoped to those groups so your changes remain reproducible and procedural.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Color faces on a box
Procedure
1) Add Box SOP inside a Geometry node.
2) Add Group SOP, set Group Type = Primitives, select a face, name it face_red.
3) Add Attribute Create: Class = Vertex, Name = Cd, Type = Vector, Size = 3, Value = 1,0,0; Group = face_red.
4) Repeat for face_blue with Value = 0,0,1.
5) Add Color SOP set to From Attributes and open Geometry Spreadsheet to verify Cd values.
Scenario card
You want two faces colored differently for export to a game engine that reads vertex color attributes. This workflow ensures each face's vertices carry the intended color.
Key Takeaway

Groups + Attribute Create = reproducible per-area edits. Use Vertex class for per-face vertex color when points are shared.

screens.title: Groups and the Group SOP
screens.narratorSegment: Groups are Houdini's named selections — they let you mark points, primitives or edges so you can restrict operations to those components. Use the Group SOP to build these selections. You can create groups manually by selecting components in the viewport and committing the selection with a descriptive name, or you can create them procedurally using methods like bounding boxes, normal angle thresholds, ranges or expressions. For instance, a bounding box base group can select all points within a volume, useful when you want to affect only geometry inside that box. Group-by-normal or angle-based methods let you target sharp edges or faces based on orientation. The Group Type parameter determines whether the group applies to points, primitives, edges or other components. Many nodes downstream expose a Group parameter; by naming your group and typing it into that field, that node will operate only on the group. An example workflow: create a group named damaged_panels with a normal-based selection, then use Attribute Create with Class = Primitive and Group = damaged_panels to set a material_type attribute to "damaged". A practical tip: use clear, descriptive group names to make your networks readable and maintainable, especially in larger procedural rigs.

How to create groups
Manual selections and procedural methods
  • Select primitives in the viewport and name the group (manual).
  • Use bounding boxes or ranges to select points procedurally.
  • Use normals/angle to select sharp edges or oriented faces.
  • Use expressions for parametric groups that update automatically.
Practical scenario
Create damaged_panels with Group SOP by angle or mask. Then use Attribute Create with Class = Primitive and Group = damaged_panels to set material_type = "damaged" so only those panels use the damaged material downstream.
Group Type: Primitives
Name: damaged_panels

screens.title: Combining attributes and groups in procedural pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: One of Houdini's strengths is composition: you compose small, focused nodes to build larger behavior. Groups and attributes are primary composition primitives. Many SOPs accept a Group parameter; when combined with Attribute Create you can precisely scope behavior. Consider a pipeline where you procedurally generate a building, compute curvature to find sharp panels, create a group by normal or curvature, and then write a primitive attribute named material_type with the value "damaged" for that group. Downstream a material assignment node or export routine reads material_type and applies the correct shader or export tag. Another example: create a point attribute wind_strength and use it to drive a Vellum simulation only on points within a wind zone group. The key design pattern is separation of concerns: use Group SOPs to define selection logic and Attribute Create to attach data that describes what to do with that selection. This keeps the network readable, testable, and easy to change. A common mistake is baking selection and behavior into one node; instead, name groups and write attributes so you can swap downstream behavior without redoing the selection.

Pattern: select → annotate → act
Define where, attach what, then let nodes react
  1. Create selection logic using Group SOPs (e.g., curvature, bounding box, manual).
  2. Use Attribute Create to write attributes for that selection (e.g., material_type, Cd).
  3. Downstream nodes read attributes and perform actions like shading, extrusion, or simulation.
Example: rock chipping
Use curvature to group sharp edges, name it high_curvature, then set a primitive attribute chipped = 1 for that group and run a bevel or Vellum simulation only on chipped primitives.
Key Takeaway

Design your networks so selections and data are separate — this supports reuse and safer edits.

screens.title: Troubleshooting and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: When attributes or groups don't behave as expected, a few common issues account for most problems. First, the wrong attribute class: if you need per-face variation at shared points but you create a point attribute, faces will share the same value. Second, attribute name mismatches — nodes expect exact names like Cd or uv; typos will make downstream nodes act as if the attribute was absent. Third, forgetting to scope the Attribute Create node with a Group leads to unintended writes across the whole mesh. Use the Geometry Spreadsheet repeatedly to verify class, type and values: it shows points, primitives, vertices and detail rows so you can confirm the attribute landed where you intended. Best practices include: using clear group names (face_red, damaged_panels), adding detail attributes for metadata like project_version rather than scattering global parameters as primitives, and documenting why a group or attribute exists inside the node network comments or notes. Another useful tip is to check Type and Size in Attribute Create; an integer stored as a float may behave differently downstream. Finally, when something still looks wrong, isolate the pipeline: bypass nodes until you find where the attribute disappears or is overridden. The takeaway is to validate early and name clearly so debugging is fast and reproducible.

fullNarratorScript:
In Houdini, geometry is just half the story. The other half is the data attached to that geometry — attributes. In this lesson you will learn what attributes are, the four classes they belong to, and how groups let you target portions of a mesh non-destructively. Attributes are values stored on points, primitives, vertices, or on the entire geometry. They control color, texture coordinates, normals, velocities and even custom integers or strings that downstream nodes or renderers can read. Groups are named selections that act like masks: they let you apply a node only to a portion of the mesh. A practical, hands-on example is coloring individual faces of a box by creating primitive groups and then using the Attribute Create SOP to write a vertex color attribute. You will also add a detail attribute to record project metadata, demonstrating how attributes and groups combine to make procedural modeling precise and maintainable. By the end, you’ll understand when to use point versus vertex attributes, how to avoid the common mistake of choosing the wrong attribute class, and how groups help keep your networks readable and flexible.

By the end of this chapter you will identify Houdini's four attribute classes and explain when to use each. You will be able to name common built-in attributes like position, normal, color and UVs, and describe their typical types and uses. You will create and modify attributes using the Attribute Create SOP, setting class, name, type and values appropriately. Finally, you will define and manipulate geometry groups to target nodes to specific parts of a mesh. Each objective focuses on practical skills: inspecting the Geometry Spreadsheet to confirm attributes, using the Group SOP to select components procedurally, and combining groups with Attribute Create so operations affect only the intended elements. These competencies are essential because attributes drive shading, simulation, instancing and export, while groups keep workflows non-destructive and readable. A concrete example you will practice is assigning different vertex colors to faces of a box and adding a detail attribute to track project version. Keep an eye out for the common mistake of choosing the wrong attribute class; we’ll show how that breaks downstream expectations and how to fix it.

This second objectives screen focuses on practice and avoiding mistakes. You will perform a hands-on workflow: create a box, make primitive groups for specific faces, use Attribute Create to write vertex colors for those groups, and inspect the results with the Geometry Spreadsheet and a Color SOP. We'll also add a detail attribute to record metadata like project version. As you work, you will learn to check attribute class and scope so the attribute appears where you expect it. A common pitfall is using a point class when you need vertex-level variation; this causes shared points to force identical data across faces. You will also practice naming groups clearly, which makes networks easier to read later. The skill here is reproducible setup — by the end you should be able to recreate the box workflow, confirm attributes in the spreadsheet, and explain why vertex attributes are required for per-face texture coordinates. These practical steps solidify the conceptual distinctions and set you up to apply attributes and groups in larger procedural systems.

Attributes are structured pieces of data stored on geometry components — they are not visual by themselves, but they inform how geometry looks and behaves. In Houdini, attributes can be vectors like position or color, integers, floats, or strings. The important claim is this: attributes make geometry data-driven. For example, the position attribute named P stores X, Y, Z coordinates and is updated whenever you move a point. A normal attribute N stores a surface direction used for shading and certain deformations. Color, Cd, is typically a three-component vector used by renderers or the viewport color display. Attribute types matter because they determine how downstream nodes interpret values; a vector cannot be treated the same as an integer. A concrete example: if you set Cd as a vertex attribute with different RGB values per face, the Color SOP can visualize that and a renderer will pick up those colors per vertex interpolation. A common misconception is thinking attributes are permanent or locked; they are simply data that nodes can read and overwrite. Another misconception is that attributes are only for rendering — they also control simulation parameters, instancing IDs, and export metadata. Key takeaway: think of attributes as the flexible data layer that lives on top of geometry and unlocks procedural control. How would you use a custom attribute to control the height of an extrusion? Consider where that value should be stored — point, primitive, vertex, or detail — before you create it.

Houdini organizes attributes into four classes tied to geometric components. Point attributes live on points. They are ideal for storing properties that should remain consistent for a point across all primitives that reference it, such as position, or a point-level weight. Primitive attributes are stored per primitive, like a material ID for a face or a primitive-wide flag. Use primitive attributes when the value represents an entire polygon or curve segment. Vertex attributes are stored per vertex, the combination of a point and a primitive; because of this they are essential when a shared point must carry different values per face, for instance unique UVs or vertex colors. A final class, detail attributes, is stored once for the whole geometry and is appropriate for global parameters such as a project_version or a single timestamp. A concrete scenario: to give each face of a cube a different UV layout, use vertex attributes; to mark an entire face as 'damaged' use a primitive attribute. A common misconception is that point attributes always give more precision — they do not; vertex attributes give independent data per face at shared points. When deciding where to store a value, ask: should this data vary per-primitive, per-point, per-vertex, or be global? That question usually reveals the correct class.

Several built-in attributes appear in most Houdini workflows. Position, named P, is a three-component vector representing a point's coordinates in space; moving a point changes P. Normal, N, is also a vector that indicates surface orientation and is heavily used by shading and orientation-sensitive operations. Cd is the conventional color attribute; it is typically a vector of three components (RGB) and can be stored as point, primitive or vertex depending on the needed variation. The uv attribute stores 2D texture coordinates and is commonly a vector of size two; because textures often differ per-face at shared points, uv is frequently stored as a vertex attribute. Velocity, often denoted v, is a vector used in simulation contexts to represent motion and is usually a point attribute when per-point motion is needed. Understanding the semantics and expected type for each built-in attribute helps you avoid mismatches — for instance, a shader will expect Cd to be present and named correctly, while UV mapping tools expect uv in the right class. A practical example: if you set a vertex Cd per face, the viewport displays each face in its color after you apply Color from Attributes. Misconception to watch: Cd stored as a detail attribute will not give per-face color; detail is global and unsuitable for per-component variations.

The Attribute Create SOP is the tool you use when you want to make a new attribute or set default values for an existing one. Its key parameters you must set deliberately are Class, Name, Type, Size, Value, and optionally Group. Class selects the attribute scope — point, primitive, vertex, or detail. Name is the attribute identifier, like Cd or project_version. Type and Size define whether the attribute is integer, float, string or vector and how many components it holds. Value sets the default or constant written by the node. The Group parameter scopes the write to only those components belonging to a named selection. A typical workflow is: create a Group SOP to build the selection; place Attribute Create after it and type the group name into Attribute Create's Group field so only that selection receives the new attribute. For example, to color a face red: set Class to Vertex, Name to Cd, Type to Vector, Size to 3, Value to 1,0,0, and set Group to face_red. A common mistake is forgetting to set Class correctly — if you choose Point instead of Vertex, shared points will force the same color across faces. Another subtlety: when creating detail attributes, Size still matters; a single integer detail uses Size 1. Always inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet after creating attributes to confirm class, type and values. That quick check saves time debugging downstream nodes that expect attributes in a particular scope.

Let's walk through the box example step by step so you can run it yourself and immediately see attributes appear. Start with a Box SOP and dive inside the geometry context. Add a Group SOP and set Group Type to Primitives. In the viewport select a single face and name the group face_red. This creates a named selection that other nodes can reference. Next add an Attribute Create SOP. Choose Class = Vertex, Name = Cd, Type = Vector, Size = 3, and set Value = 1,0,0. In Attribute Create's Group field, type face_red so the write only affects vertices belonging to that face. Repeat the Group + Attribute Create steps to create face_blue with Cd = 0,0,1. Then add a Color SOP set to From Attributes to visualize. Finally open the Geometry Spreadsheet to inspect vertex rows and confirm Cd values on the vertices that belong to your face groups. A common confusion is expecting point-level Cd to let two faces sharing a point have different colors — that will not work. The vertex class is required for per-face color when points are shared. The practical takeaway is to build your selection with groups, then write attributes scoped to those groups so your changes remain reproducible and procedural.

Groups are Houdini's named selections — they let you mark points, primitives or edges so you can restrict operations to those components. Use the Group SOP to build these selections. You can create groups manually by selecting components in the viewport and committing the selection with a descriptive name, or you can create them procedurally using methods like bounding boxes, normal angle thresholds, ranges or expressions. For instance, a bounding box base group can select all points within a volume, useful when you want to affect only geometry inside that box. Group-by-normal or angle-based methods let you target sharp edges or faces based on orientation. The Group Type parameter determines whether the group applies to points, primitives, edges or other components. Many nodes downstream expose a Group parameter; by naming your group and typing it into that field, that node will operate only on the group. An example workflow: create a group named damaged_panels with a normal-based selection, then use Attribute Create with Class = Primitive and Group = damaged_panels to set a material_type attribute to "damaged". A practical tip: use clear, descriptive group names to make your networks readable and maintainable, especially in larger procedural rigs.

One of Houdini's strengths is composition: you compose small, focused nodes to build larger behavior. Groups and attributes are primary composition primitives. Many SOPs accept a Group parameter; when combined with Attribute Create you can precisely scope behavior. Consider a pipeline where you procedurally generate a building, compute curvature to find sharp panels, create a group by normal or curvature, and then write a primitive attribute named material_type with the value "damaged" for that group. Downstream a material assignment node or export routine reads material_type and applies the correct shader or export tag. Another example: create a point attribute wind_strength and use it to drive a Vellum simulation only on points within a wind zone group. The key design pattern is separation of concerns: use Group SOPs to define selection logic and Attribute Create to attach data that describes what to do with that selection. This keeps the network readable, testable, and easy to change. A common mistake is baking selection and behavior into one node; instead, name groups and write attributes so you can swap downstream behavior without redoing the selection.

When attributes or groups don't behave as expected, a few common issues account for most problems. First, the wrong attribute class: if you need per-face variation at shared points but you create a point attribute, faces will share the same value. Second, attribute name mismatches — nodes expect exact names like Cd or uv; typos will make downstream nodes act as if the attribute was absent. Third, forgetting to scope the Attribute Create node with a Group leads to unintended writes across the whole mesh. Use the Geometry Spreadsheet repeatedly to verify class, type and values: it shows points, primitives, vertices and detail rows so you can confirm the attribute landed where you intended. Best practices include: using clear group names (face_red, damaged_panels), adding detail attributes for metadata like project_version rather than scattering global parameters as primitives, and documenting why a group or attribute exists inside the node network comments or notes. Another useful tip is to check Type and Size in Attribute Create; an integer stored as a float may behave differently downstream. Finally, when something still looks wrong, isolate the pipeline: bypass nodes until you find where the attribute disappears or is overridden. The takeaway is to validate early and name clearly so debugging is fast and reproducible.

Second, the four attribute classes — point, primitive, vertex, and detail — map to different geometric granularities, and choosing the right class is crucial. Third, groups are named selections used as masks so nodes can operate only on intended components; combine groups with Attribute Create to annotate selected components with new data. Finally, use the Geometry Spreadsheet to verify attributes, and adopt clear naming and scoping conventions. A concrete mental model: selection logic lives in groups, data lives in attributes, and nodes read that data to perform shading, simulation or export. Keep these principles in mind and you'll make robust, non-destructive procedural systems that are easier to debug and reuse.
